claims.sentence: Asthma is a common long-term condition that affects the airways.
claims.evidence: NHS asthma page: asthma is a long-term airway condition. 'Common' not stated in retrieved text.
claims.newSentence: Asthma is a long-term condition that affects the airways.

claims.sentence: The NHS says the main symptoms are wheezing, coughing, shortness of breath and a tight chest, and that they often come and go.
claims.evidence: NHS asthma page: wheezing, coughing, breathlessness and chest tightness; symptoms can come and go.

claims.sentence: Symptoms range from mild to severe, and they can be set off by triggers such as allergies, cold air, exercise and infections.
claims.evidence: Retrieved triggers: exercise, cold air, air pollution, allergens such as pollen or dust. 'Mild to severe' and 'infections' not backed on the NHS asthma page (viruses such as flu making asthma worse came from other NHS pages).
claims.newSentence: Common triggers include exercise, cold air, air pollution and allergens such as pollen or dust.

claims.sentence: The NHS says the exact cause of asthma is not fully understood, but allergies, a family history of asthma or allergies, and early-life exposure to air pollution or cigarette smoke are among the factors linked with it.
claims.evidence: NHS: not fully understood what causes asthma; risk factors include allergies such as eczema or hay fever, family history, premature birth, childhood exposure to air pollution or cigarette smoke.

claims.sentence: COPD, short for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, is the name for a group of lung conditions that cause breathing difficulties.
claims.evidence: NHS 111 Wales: COPD is an umbrella term including emphysema and chronic bronchitis; NHS COPD page covers breathing symptoms.

claims.sentence: It includes emphysema and chronic bronchitis.
claims.evidence: NHS 111 Wales and MedlinePlus: COPD includes emphysema and chronic bronchitis.

claims.sentence: The NHS says the main cause is smoking, although it can sometimes affect people who have never smoked.
claims.evidence: NHS 111 Wales: mainly affects adults who smoke; some cases from long-term fumes or dust or a rare genetic cause. Attributed to NHS 111 Wales rather than the England page.

claims.sentence: Typical symptoms are breathlessness on exertion, a persistent chesty cough with phlegm, frequent chest infections and wheeze.
claims.evidence: NHS COPD overview: breathlessness during activity, persistent chesty cough with phlegm, frequent chest infections, persistent wheezing.

claims.sentence: They tend to get worse over time.
claims.evidence: NHS: without treatment symptoms usually get progressively worse.

claims.sentence: The two conditions can look alike, and some people have both.
claims.evidence: Not retrieved. NICE NG115 says untreated COPD and asthma are frequently distinguishable on history and examination in people presenting for the first time. 'Some people have both' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: NICE says that when someone first presents with symptoms, untreated COPD and asthma can frequently be told apart from the person's history and an examination.

claims.sentence: NICE advises using features from the person's history to help tell them apart: smoking history, the age when symptoms began, whether breathlessness is persistent and progressive or variable, and whether symptoms vary from day to day or wake the person at night.
claims.evidence: NICE NG115: use features from history and examination 'such as those listed in table 3'. The table contents were not retrieved, so the specific list is unbacked.
claims.newSentence: NICE advises using features from the person's history and examination to help tell the two conditions apart.

claims.sentence: Breathing tests help.
claims.evidence: NICE: COPD diagnosis supported by spirometry; NHS: asthma diagnosis uses lung function tests.

claims.sentence: Spirometry measures how much air a person can blow out and how fast, and it is used for both conditions.
claims.evidence: NICE NG115: COPD suspected from symptoms and signs and supported by spirometry. NICE NG245 draft evidence review: spirometry not a standalone test for asthma; many people with asthma have normal spirometry at the time. Description of the measurement itself not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: Spirometry is a breathing test that supports a diagnosis of COPD, and lung function tests also form part of diagnosing asthma, although a normal result does not always rule asthma out.

claims.sentence: The site's spirometry page explains the test, and the laboratory or clinic report shows the reference values used.
claims.evidence: Meta pointer to site page is harmless but the clause about reports showing reference values is not backed; NICE sources note thresholds differ between guidance and clinical bodies.
claims.newSentence: The site's spirometry page explains the test.

claims.sentence: Because symptoms vary and breathing problems have more than one cause, the NHS notes that diagnosing asthma can take time.
claims.evidence: NHS: asthma can take some time to diagnose because symptoms often vary over time and breathing problems can have different causes.

claims.sentence: Asthma has no cure, but the NHS says the main treatment is medicine breathed in through an inhaler, which works well for most people.
claims.evidence: Inhalers are the main treatment (NHS). 'No cure' and 'works well for most people' not retrieved for asthma.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says inhalers are the main treatment for asthma.

claims.sentence: Reliever inhalers ease symptoms when they occur, and preventer inhalers are used regularly to reduce them.
claims.evidence: NHS: reliever inhalers are used when symptoms occur; preventer inhalers are taken daily.

claims.sentence: An asthma action plan is usually agreed with a doctor or asthma nurse.
claims.evidence: NHS: you will usually create a personal action plan with a doctor or asthma nurse.

claims.sentence: COPD cannot be reversed, but its progression can be slowed, and stopping smoking is one of the most effective steps.
claims.evidence: NHS: no cure for COPD; treatment can help slow progression and control symptoms; stopping smoking is the most important step for people who smoke. 'Cannot be reversed' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: There is currently no cure for COPD, but treatment can help slow its progression and control symptoms, and for people who smoke, stopping smoking is the most important step.

claims.sentence: Treatment mainly relieves symptoms, with inhalers, and pulmonary rehabilitation may help people become more active.
claims.evidence: NHS: inhalers and medicines ease breathing; pulmonary rehabilitation (exercise and education) can improve how far you can exercise before becoming breathless.

claims.sentence: Asthma attacks can be life-threatening.
claims.evidence: NHS: an asthma attack is when symptoms are severe and it is difficult to breathe, which can be life-threatening.

claims.sentence: The NHS says urgent medical help is needed if symptoms get worse or if the reliever inhaler stops working, and the route for that is 999.
claims.evidence: NHS: call 999 if you do not feel better after taking the maximum dose of a reliever inhaler, feel worse at any time, or have no inhaler. 'Stops working' wording not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: During an asthma attack, the NHS says to call 999 if the person does not feel better after using their reliever inhaler as directed, if they feel worse at any time, or if they do not have an inhaler.

claims.sentence: For COPD, sudden worsening breathlessness is also a reason to seek urgent help.
claims.evidence: NHS describes COPD flare-ups (symptoms suddenly get worse) but no urgent-care route was retrieved; urgency statement lacks 999/NHS 111/GP route.
claims.newSentence: COPD symptoms can suddenly get worse in what is called a flare-up. A person unsure what to do can contact their GP or NHS 111 for advice, and 999 is for emergencies.

claims.sentence: NHS 111 can advise when it is unclear how serious a flare-up is.
claims.evidence: General description of the NHS 111 service; not on a retrieved page but harmless and provides a route to care.

claims.sentence: A GP appointment is the route for new or persistent breathing symptoms, so that the cause can be found.
claims.evidence: Not retrieved. NHS: asthma diagnosis draws on symptoms, listening to the chest and lung function tests; NICE: COPD suspected from symptoms and signs and supported by spirometry.
claims.newSentence: A GP can look into new or ongoing breathing problems, because both conditions are diagnosed using symptoms, an examination and lung function tests.

claims.sentence: Both conditions are reviewed regularly by a GP or nurse.
claims.evidence: Asthma reviews and discussing flu jabs at them found in NHS trust/ICB guidance; COPD review not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: People with asthma are offered regular asthma reviews, where things such as flu vaccination can be discussed.

claims.sentence: Not smoking, and avoiding known triggers for asthma, are common themes in NHS advice.
claims.evidence: NHS: stopping smoking is the most important step in COPD for people who smoke. Avoiding asthma triggers as NHS advice not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: For people with COPD who smoke, the NHS says stopping smoking is the most important step.

claims.sentence: Vaccinations against flu and some other infections are often offered to people with long-term lung conditions, because chest infections can cause flare-ups.
claims.evidence: NHS 'living with COPD': everyone with COPD is encouraged to have the annual flu jab and one-off pneumococcal vaccination. Asthma: viruses such as flu can make symptoms worse; some people with asthma qualify for free flu vaccine. 'Chest infections cause flare-ups' for COPD not stated.
claims.newSentence: The NHS encourages people with COPD to have the yearly flu jab and a one-off pneumococcal vaccination, and for asthma it advises vaccinations such as the flu vaccine because viruses such as flu can make asthma symptoms worse.

claims.sentence: The care team can explain what applies in each case.
claims.evidence: Only retrieved: flu jabs can be discussed at an asthma review.
claims.newSentence: Flu jabs can be discussed at an asthma review.

claims.sentence: Asthma symptoms come and go and vary between people, while COPD symptoms are usually more persistent and tend to worsen over time.
claims.evidence: Asthma symptoms can come and go (NHS); COPD symptoms usually get progressively worse without treatment. 'Vary between people' and 'more persistent' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: Asthma symptoms can come and go, while COPD symptoms usually get progressively worse without treatment.

claims.sentence: The main cause of COPD is smoking, though it can affect people who have never smoked.
claims.evidence: As c07 (NHS 111 Wales, MedlinePlus).

claims.sentence: Clinicians use history, age at onset and breathing tests such as spirometry to tell the two apart.
claims.evidence: NICE: history and examination features, spirometry supports COPD diagnosis. 'Age at onset' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: Clinicians use a person's history, an examination and breathing tests such as spirometry to tell the two apart.

claims.sentence: Asthma is mainly treated with inhalers; COPD cannot be reversed, but treatment and stopping smoking can slow it.
claims.evidence: Inhalers main treatment for asthma (NHS); COPD: no cure, treatment can slow progression. 'Cannot be reversed' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: Asthma is mainly treated with inhalers; COPD has no cure, but treatment and stopping smoking can help slow it.

claims.sentence: A reliever inhaler that stops working during an attack is an emergency: the NHS says to call 999.
claims.evidence: NHS: call 999 if not better after the maximum dose of reliever, if feeling worse, or with no inhaler. 'Stops working' wording not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: In an asthma attack, call 999 if you do not feel better after using your reliever inhaler as directed, or if you feel worse at any time.

claims.sentence: Asthma causes variable, reversible airway narrowing that often starts young; COPD is mostly smoking-related and worsens over time.
claims.evidence: 'Reversible' and 'often starts young' not retrieved. Asthma symptoms come and go; COPD mainly affects people who smoke and usually gets worse.
claims.newSentence: Asthma is a long-term airway condition whose symptoms come and go; COPD is mostly smoking-related and tends to get worse over time.

notes: Only 5 searches used. NICE NG115 table 3 and NG245 final history features were not retrieved, so the feature list was cut. NHS England COPD main page text came through only as search summary; some COPD facts are attributed to NHS 111 Wales and MedlinePlus. Asthma annual-review and flu-eligibility details came from NHS trust/ICB documents, not the main NHS asthma page; no frequency or cut-offs added. Puff counts for asthma attacks differ between sources and were deliberately not used.
